metric.why: Liquid-cooled AI racks with coolant, manifolds, and batteries are dramatically heavier than the enterprise racks most buildings were engineered for. Retrofit projects hit structural limits before electrical ones more often than the industry expected.
metric.definition: The structural weight the raised floor or slab supports per square foot, against the actual weight of installed racks.

reading.body:
Retrofit data centers hit structural weight limits before electrical ones more often than expected, because liquid-cooled AI racks with coolant, manifolds, and batteries exceed the floor loading capacity most buildings were engineered to support.

The mismatch between legacy building design and modern thermal density matters because it compresses the timeline for AI deployment. A facility can have spare power and cooling capacity yet remain unusable if the raised floor or slab cannot bear the load per square foot. This is a buildings problem, not an electrical one, and it cannot be solved by adding generators or chillers.

The constraint also shapes which data centers will scale. Older facilities with lower original load ratings hit this limit first during retrofit. Newer construction or purpose-built facilities designed for heavy racks avoid it. This splits the usable retrofit stock and forces new build, which takes years.

This metric does not capture the cost to reinforce floors, the timeline delays from structural engineering, or how many planned AI deployments have stalled at this stage. It measures the gap between nameplate capacity and actual occupancy. Whether that gap can be closed, and how quickly, depends on civil engineering constraints that are outside the data center operator's control.
